articles.title: MLB Contract, Team Predictions for Each Player Who Rejected Qualifying Offer
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's offseason began with eight players receiving a one-year, $23.15M qualifying offer. Six declined; five remain on the market, while Jake Bauers has already signed with Boston.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball's offseason began with eight players receiving a one-year, $23.15M qualifying offer. Six declined; five remain on the market, while Jake Bauers has already signed with Boston.

David Bednar accepting the one-year offer from the Yankees was pretty surprising, especially after Adrián Morejón rejected his. Ryan Jeffers remaining with the Twins was less of a stunner, but still a bit unexpected.

But those other new free agents now come with an added cost if they sign somewhere new. The exact compensation for the team losing the free agent and the penalty paid by the signing team depends on whether each pays a luxury tax or benefits from revenue sharing.

However, that's a minor hurdle in the grand scheme of things, particularly in regard to the likes of Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki who could be headed for nine-figure contracts.

Now that these players are actually available to the highest bidder, though, let's take an updated look at projected contracts and plausible landing spots.

For each, we've included contract projections from a trio of sources— MLB Trade Rumors , ESPN's Kiley McDaniel and our own Tim Kelly —before offering up an estimate of our own.

2026 Stats : .281/.381/.484, 26 HR, 79 RBI, 26 SB, 5.7 bWAR

Other Projections : 4/$100M (MLBTR); 4/$90M (ESPN); 5/$140M (Kelly)

Our Prediction : 4 years, $112M with the Philadelphia Phillies

Randy Arozarena has reeled off six consecutive 20/20 seasons.

He's one of six players with at least 130 home runs and 130 stolen bases since the beginning of 2021, the others being Shohei Ohtani, José Ramírez, Trea Turner, Fernando Tatis Jr. and Julio Rodríguez—each of whom is already playing on a contract with a total face value of at least $175M.

Arozarena also just had the best overall season of his career, posting an OPS of .865 after five consecutive years in the .720-.815 range. He even scored an AL-best 113 runs, while the Mariners flirted with ranking dead last in the majors in scoring.

However, he turns 32 in February, so the expectation is that he's headed for a four-year, maybe five-year deal—in contrast to last winter when everyone was trying to guess what a 29-year-old Kyle Tucker might get on a decade-long contract as the top position player on the market.

As far as the landing spot is concerned, a lot of teams figure to be in on Arozarena.

Among the five teams who ran up a total bill north of $350M last season and seemingly have no spending limit, both Toronto and Philadelphia would greatly benefit from an upgrade in left field. Slightly lower in the payroll rankings, the Cubs, Padres, Braves, Astros, Tigers, Diamondbacks and Orioles could all use a corner outfielder. Goodness knows the Mariners also have an Arozarena-sized hole in left field now, too. Boston might still be in the mix, too, even after its recent acquisition of Jake Bauers.

It feels like this is going to be the Phillies' big splash, though. 2027 is probably the last realistic year of their championship window, and they're likely to run up their biggest luxury tax payment yet in hopes of winning one. And not having a reliable right-handed bat (or a reliable outfielder in general) was one of the biggest things holding them back in 2026.

2026 Stats : .266/.389/.484, 26 HR, 86 RBI, 11 SB, 3.3 bWAR

Other Projections : 1/$23.15M (MLBTR); 3/$52.5M (ESPN); 1/$23.15M (Kelly)

Already Signed : 4 years, $58M with the Boston Red Sox

If anybody was going to take the qualifying offer, the assumption was that Jake Bauers would be the one. His breakout season was among the most unexpected in recent memory: He posted 3.3 WAR after totaling minus-1.2 through his first six seasons.

Instead, he turned down the offer and secured a four-year deal from Boston.

Both the length of the contract and the landing spot were pretty unexpected.

The Red Sox already have Willson Contreras for one more year to man first base, as well as a surplus of corner outfielders. There has been talk (for about two years at this point) of Jarren Duran being on the trade block, but one would assume they're also now looking to part with Masataka Yoshida, paving the way for Bauers and Contreras to tag team the 1B and DH spots.

We'll let them figure that part out, but if Bauers can replicate his 2026 campaign, what a boon that would be for the Red Sox, who didn't have a ton of offense this past season outside of Contreras and that three-week stretch in which Mickey Gasper randomly became Mickey Mantle.

2026 Stats : .260/.331/.493, 35 HR, 96 RBI, 5.3 bWAR

Other Projections : 3/$69M (MLBTR); 4/$80M (ESPN); 3/$75.3M (Kelly)

Our Prediction : 3 years, $66M with the Pittsburgh Pirates

I've made this point in previous articles already this offseason, but it bears repeating: There is no good reason to assume that a player is unlikely to re-sign with the same team just because he declines a qualifying offer.

In fact, of the 57 players who rejected a qualifying offer over the previous six offseasons, 16 of them (28.1 percent) ended up re-signing.

So, Brandon Lowe declining Pittsburgh's qualifying offer doesn't necessarily mean the door to a reunion has been closed.

Rather, this kind of looks like a case where the qualifying offer makes it more likely that he stays with Pittsburgh.

After all, the second base market is robust this offseason with Gleyber Torres, Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Luis Arraez available to the highest bidder. While Lowe is arguably the best of the bunch, is he so clearly the best that teams are going to be willing to part with a draft pick (or multiple picks) in order to prioritize him?

Also, we're talking about a second baseman who will turn 33 shortly before the All-Star break and has a fairly robust injury history. He played 150 games in 2026, but averaged 104 over the previous four seasons.

Can teams justify giving him a contract of four or more years? And, if not, doesn't the notion of giving up some draft capital to sign him feel a bit more foolish?

Maybe the Yankees do it anyway, as they work on revamping their infield. The Red Sox might also be in the mix. But as long as the Pirates don't egregiously lowball Lowe, staying in Pittsburgh on a three-year deal feels like the likeliest outcome here.

2026 Stats : 86.0 IP, 2.83 ERA, 2.37 FIP, 1.08 WHIP, 11.2 K/9, 1.9 bWAR

Other Projections : 5/$80M (MLBTR); 4/$88M (ESPN); 4/$80M (Kelly)

Our Prediction : 4 years, $76M with the Chicago White Sox

With just eight career saves and no interest in transitioning to the starting rotation, the market for Adrián Morejón is going to be nothing short of fascinating.

Over the past three years, Morejón has been one of the most dominant pitchers in the majors, boasting a sub-2.60 mark in both ERA (2.58) and FIP (2.46).

The only others with at least 200 innings of work who can say the same are 2026 NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski, 2024 NL Cy Young winner Chris Sale, 2024-25 AL Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal and Cleveland's fantastic set-up man-turned-closer Cade Smith.

But, historically speaking, relievers don't get paid the big bucks unless they're closers.

At any rate, six relievers received an AAV of at least $13M in free agency last offseason, and each of them already had at least 75 career saves. Good luck trying to find the last time a middle reliever received one of the two biggest bullpen contracts in a given offseason cycle.

We all expect Morejón to be an exception to the rule, but how big of one?

The White Sox could be a fantastic landing spot, especially given the recent reports that they plan to move Grant Taylor to the starting rotation. However, we're talking about a franchise that has never signed a pitcher (free agent or extension) to a contract of more than $65M.

Is Morejón going to be where they break that cycle?

If not, the other team in Chicago figures to be very much in the bidding war, too.

2026 Stats : 169.2 IP, 4.03 ERA, 3.45 FIP, 1.19 WHIP, 8.3 K/9, 2.2 bWAR

Other Projections : 5/$115M (MLBTR); 4/$76M (ESPN); 5/$110M (Kelly)

Our Prediction : 4 years, $104M with the Chicago Cubs

Trevor Rogers has been all over the map throughout his career, which makes his market in free agency maybe the most intriguing of all.

Across the 2020, 2022 and 2024 seasons, he made 55 starts with a 5.28 ERA and a combined 0.2 bWAR. He also missed almost all of 2023 because of biceps and lat injuries.

He was otherwise masterful in 2026, though, this after posting a scintillating 1.81 ERA across his 18 starts in 2025. And back in 2021, he finished second in the NL Rookie of the Year vote with a 2.64 ERA in 25 starts.

When he's on point, not many pitchers are better.

But if he gets a five-year deal, how many of those years will actually be high quality?

An intriguing comp for Rogers' market is Jesús Luzardo, who has also had a few brutal seasons due to injury and/or ineffectiveness, but who has shown a repeated ability to be relentlessly dominant for months at a time.

Luzardo got a five-year, $135M extension from the Phillies prior to this past season, and he'd presumably be worth even more right now after putting together what was the best year of his career in 2026.

They're the same age, each turning 29 this fall. And Rogers' current career bWAR of 11.1 is identical to what Luzardo's career mark was when he signed his extension.

So, is everyone a bit low on Rogers, projecting him for an AAV in the $19M-$23M range?

Could he actually fetch something closer to $30M once Tarik Skubal signs his monster deal and the teams who come up short in that bidding war become desperate to land an ace-caliber arm?

Or has he been inconsistent enough that teams will be reluctant to give him nine figures?

My hunch is that the Cubs want him more badly than most. They need to rebuild their starting rotation, almost from scratch, and Rogers' home run rate has been at or below 1.01 per nine innings pitched in each of the past four seasons. Bringing him in to replace Shota Imanaga would be a dream come true.

2026 Stats : .270/.368/.473, 26 HR, 86 RBI, 5.1 bWAR

Other Projections : 4/$105M (MLBTR); 4/$90M (ESPN); 5/$145M (Kelly)

Our Prediction : 4 years, $108M with the Toronto Blue Jays

At the plate, Seiya Suzuki has been Mr. Consistency.

In each of the past four seasons, he has both logged enough plate appearances to qualify for a batting title and posted an OPS of at least .800. The only other players who can say the same are Shohei Ohtani, Bobby Witt Jr., Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Rafael Devers.

Granted, each of those other players has had multiple seasons with an OPS north of .850 while Suzuki has maxed out at .848. That's why he has yet to be named an All-Star: He's more of a "constant B+ or A-" type of offensive weapon than a 'best on the planet' sort of superstar.

But in a world of boxes of variety chocolates, why not pursue the bag of KitKats that you know to be consistently delicious?

What's more, Suzuki just had the best defensive season of his career in right field, posting a career-high 14 Defensive Runs Saved, and could be a major asset there. Still, teams banking on that element of his game should note that his defensive ratings were generally average or below average over his first four MLB seasons.

Like Randy Arozarena, though, he's heading into his age-32 season and is probably also looking at a four- or five-year deal at around $25M apiece.

The list of suitors should be similar to those we mentioned for Arozarena. However, teams like the Phillies and Astros that already have a full-time DH would figure to be less interested in Suzuki.

We'll go with the Blue Jays for his landing spot, as they just lost a full-time DH making roughly $25M per year in George Springer and also no longer have three outfielders (Daulton Varsho, Myles Straw and Jesús Sánchez) who each appeared in at least 99 games for them in 2026.

Suzuki could play RF for them on a regular basis if Anthony Santander continues to be a completely sunk cost, or he might just be the plan at DH for years to come.

articles.title: New Tarik Skubal Rumors on Dodgers & Blue Jays Meetings as MLB Teams 'Willing to Break the Bank'
articles.summary: The week is still young, but Tarik Skubal has been busy after meeting with two more teams on Tuesday as he makes the rounds in free agency looking to secure the richest deal for a pitcher in MLB history.
articles.body:
The week is still young, but Tarik Skubal has been busy after meeting with two more teams on Tuesday as he makes the rounds in free agency looking to secure the richest deal for a pitcher in MLB history.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , Skubal met with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays on Tuesday after talking to the New York Mets on Monday.

Passan noted Skubal's decision could come sooner than later with teams "willing to break the bank" for the two-time AL Cy Young winner.

The Mets held an in-person meeting with Skubal that Jon Heyman of the New York Post and MLB Network reported "went very well" despite no formal offer being made at the time.

Heyman added the "expectation" is Skubal will sign before the expected lockout begins at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1.

According to Passan, the Mets came away from their visit with Skubal "impressed" and it reinforced their "status as favorites" to sign him.

The Dodgers, Blue Jays and San Diego Padres are the other known teams expected to be in the mix, with Heyman also citing two mystery teams that could be involved.

Per The Athletic's Jim Bowden , teams expect Skubal's contract to land anywhere in the range of $350 to $500 million.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds the record for richest pitcher contract on his 12-year, $325 million deal with the Dodgers. Zack Wheeler of the Philadelphia Phillies is the highest-paid pitcher by average annual salary at $42 million.

Skubal's familiarity with the Dodgers could give them an edge, though they don't appear inclined to go as far on a contract in terms of total value as he might prefer.

Katie Woo of The Athletic reported last week the Dodgers' interest in bringing Skubal back hinges on his willingness to accept a shorter offer than he is likely to receive from other clubs.

The Blue Jays are in a good position to make a big move with more than $70 million coming off the payroll among their 10 free agents. They also have a need because their rotation depth behind Dylan Cease is not strong.

José Soriano and Spencer Arrighetti, their two big midseason acquisitions, both had an ERA over 5.00 in 77 combined innings with Toronto. Trey Yesavage struggled to throw strikes consistently with 47 walks in 97.2 innings due to two IL stints for shoulder and knee injuries.

The Blue Jays also have some pressure to do something significant coming off a last-place finish in the AL East after reaching the World Series in 2025.

Skubal finished the 2026 season with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings in 26 starts between the Dodgers and Detroit Tigers. It was his third consecutive year with a sub-3.00 ERA, more than 10 strikeouts per nine innings and at least 150 innings.

articles.title: MLB Teams 'Balking at' Randy Arozarena's $100M+ Contract Ask, New Free-Agency Rumors Reveal
articles.summary: Coming off the best year of his career and being one of the few prominent hitters available in free agency, Randy Arozarena is hoping to cash in big even if it means waiting to sign until after MLB's labor situation gets resolved.
articles.body:
Coming off the best year of his career and being one of the few prominent hitters available in free agency, Randy Arozarena is hoping to cash in big even if it means waiting to sign until after MLB's labor situation gets resolved.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , Arozarena's current desire for "well over $100 million" has interested teams "balking" at that price tag and it could lead to him staying on the market until after the expected lockout begins:

"He has suitors, yes, but they are balking at his ask of well over $100 million, and with the abbreviated time before the lockout, compromise can be difficult to come by. This doesn't mean Arozarena won't sign. Losing out on another player or two can prompt a team to amend its offer — or just go on tilt. But unless something changes, he could be the Freddie Freeman of this class, ready to cash in once the lockout lifts."

Arozarena is in a tricky spot because his offensive resume suggests he is a player who could warrant that type of an investment from a team.

A three-time All-Star, including each of the last two years, Arozarena has been a well-above-average hitter by wRC+ every season of his career. His worst single-season mark in that category was 120 in 2025.

As a comparison, Alex Bregman had three seasons with a wRC+ of 120 or worse from 2017 to '24. He signed a five-year, $175 million deal with the Chicago Cubs last offseason going into his age-32 season in 2026.

Arozarena will be going into his age-32 season in 2027. He is coming off his best year with a .281/.381/.484 slash line, 26 homers and 26 stolen bases in 154 games for the Seattle Mariners to finish eighth in AL MVP voting.

The difference between Arozarena and Bregman comes in primarily on defense. Bregman remains a high-level glove at third base. Arozarena has been below-average in the outfield for most of his career. He ranks 43rd out of 49 qualified outfielders in outs above average since the start of 2024.

Even with the defensive limitations, though, Arozarena has been incredibly consistent at the plate. He has six consecutive years with at least 20 homers and 20 stolen bases.

A contract of at least $100 million is risky for a player who is not far away from entering his mid-30s and will likely move to DH sooner than later, but he should be able to maintain his value with the bat for at least the next couple of years.

articles.title: Top 2026 MLB Free Agents Available and Latest Rumors, Predictions
articles.summary: The Tarik Skubal sweepstakes is the story dominating MLB free agency.
articles.body:
The Tarik Skubal sweepstakes is the story dominating MLB free agency.

The two-time Cy Young Award winner is far and away the top free agent in the sport. His market appears to be down to a handful of teams.

Skubal's reportedly met with the New York Mets, Toronto Blue Jays and Los Angeles Dodgers already this week, per ESPN's Jeff Passan. The San Diego Padres are on the shortlist for a meeting as well.

Skubal's decision is the most anticipated one in the sport. Once he signs, the market could move fast, especially on the pitching side for teams that missed out on the star left-hander.

Trevor Rogers, Michael King and Freddy Peralta are among the best non-Skubal pitchers on the market. They should generate some interest in the coming weeks.

As for the hitters, Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena are the top players available. Teruaki Sato, a 27-year-old from Japan, is also at the top of the list for teams that need hitting.

ESPN's Jeff Passan expects Tarik Skubal to sign the "largest deal for a pitcher in baseball history."

The star southpaw already talked with the Mets, Dodgers and Blue Jays and the Padres are on deck, per Passan.

ESPN's Buster Olney added on Wednesday morning that "the expectation of some involved in the Tarik Skubal negotiations: in the end, the bidding will pit the Mets vs the Blue Jays.

The Dodgers should never be truly counted out when it comes to one of the game's biggest stars, but they need a power arm less than the Mets and Blue Jays do.

The Mets could use a star at the top of their rotation to complement the young stars they already have at the major-league level. Adding Skubal would help the Mets compete with the Philadelphia Phillies and their deep rotation in the National League East.

Toronto already has Dylan Cease, Jose Soriano and Trey Yesavage in its rotation. Landing Skubal would give the Blue Jays one of the best rotations in the sport.

All of the teams involved in the Skubal sweepstakes have not been shy about spending. The Mets need him the most, but the Blue Jays need to make a splash to get back on track after a rough 2026.

Again, the Dodgers should never be counted out of anything, but the Mets and Blue Jays are in need of Skubal. The Mets are the more desperate of those two teams and that could drive them to land the premier free agent.

Prediction: Tarik Skubal Lands With Mets

According to ESPN's Jeff Passan , the San Diego Padres met with Seiya Suzuki on Monday and "could be the favorites to add him."

Suzuki officially became a free agent earlier this week when he declined the qualifying offer from the Chicago Cubs.

The 32-year-old is viewed as one of the best hitters available in a market that doesn't have too many standout sluggers.

Suzuki hit at least 20 home runs in four of his five season with the Cubs and he knocked in 189 runs over the last two seasons.

He would be an excellent addition to the Padres lineup. He'd also allow Fernando Tatis Jr. to move back to the infield, something Passan noted in his report.

Suzuki would be a fascinating run-producing option in the middle of the Padres lineup behind Tatis and Manny Machado.

It's one of the best possible free-agent upgrades the Padres can make in their ongoing quest to keep up with the Dodgers in the NL West.

Prediction: Seiya Suzuki Signs With Padres

Randy Arozarena is also generating interest as one of the top free-agent hitters.

According to Jon Heyman of New York Post , the New York Yankees "checked in" on the veteran outfielder.

Jon Morosi mentioned on MLB Network on Tuesday that the Baltimore Orioles, Philadelphia Phillies and Toronto Blue Jays are among the teams that be in the market for Arozarena.

Arozarena hit 73 home runs and stole 77 bases over the last three season, the last two of which he spent with the Seattle Mariners.

Philadelphia is potentially the most intriguing fit for Arozarena because it needs a right-handed outfield bat.

The Phillies tried to add more right-handed power with Adolis Garcia last offseason, but he spent the second half of the 2026 season on the injured list.

Arozarena would add more pop and speed to the middle of the Phillies order to provide some needed support for Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Co.

Prediction: Randy Arozarena Signs With Phillies

articles.title: Maikel Garcia Traded to Mariners From Royals, New MLB Rumors on Return for Former Gold Glove Winner
articles.summary: The Kansas City Royals and Seattle Mariners came together for a trade to address their specific roster needs going into the 2027 season.
articles.body:
The Kansas City Royals and Seattle Mariners came together for a trade to address their specific roster needs going into the 2027 season.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , the six-player deal is headlined by Maikel Garcia going to the Mariners and right-handed pitcher Bryce Miller coming back to Kansas City.

This trade came together after Passan reported earlier in the day that Kansas City was making Garcia available in a trade as it looked to add pitching help.

One of the biggest issues for the Royals in 2026 was a lack of depth in the rotation. Michael Wacha was the unquestioned ace of the group with a 3.32 ERA in 200.2 innings.

Noah Cameron was a solid innings-eater who wound up being their No. 2 by default. Seth Lugo, who was in the first year of a two-year, $46 million extension, finished with a career-worst 5.17 ERA in 32 starts.

Miller has been inconsistent throughout his MLB career, but his upside is high as evidenced by his 2.94 ERA in 31 starts during the 2024 season. In two season since that breakout year, he has a 4.82 ERA in 209 innings over 40 appearances.

Logan Evans is a potential depth arm for the Royals as he prepares to return after missing all of 2026 due to an elbow injury that required the internal brace surgery. The 25-year-old had a 4.32 ERA as a rookie with Seattle in 2025.

The Mariners' addition of Garcia indicates Brendan Donovan, who played primarily at third base last season, will likely move to left field with Randy Arozarena presumably not returning as a free agent.

Garcia's best tool is his defense that earned him a Gold Glove at third base in 2025. He also hit .286/.351/.449 with a career-high 16 homers at the plate that year.

The 2026 campaign was a step back offensively for Garcia with a .268/.334/.381 slash line, but he was limited to 82 games due to a variety of injuries.

James McArthur is essentially a flyer for the Mariners since he hasn't appeared in an MLB game since the 2024 season due to elbow injuries. The right-hander did appear in four minor-league games last season, finishing with a 7.36 ERA in 3.2 innings.

articles.title: Phillies showing more interest than any MLB team in 39-HR Japanese slugger
articles.summary: The Phillies seem to have the most interest in this top free agent slugger.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Phillies are in dire need of more offensive firepower. Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper are great core pieces of this offense, but their other options are subpar.

While they could try to sign someone like Seiya Suzuki or Randy Arozarena, the loss of draft picks for signing one of them might make it hard to sign either player. But fortunately, there's an obvious solution to fill their outfield hole this Fall.

Japanese Triple-Crown slugger Teruaki Sato, coming off a 39-homer season, is the perfect option. And according to ESPN's Jeff Passan , there isn't a team in MLB that is more interested in signing Sato than the Phillies.

Phillies have the most interest of any team in Teruaki Sato

"Sato is the best bat available in the class, ranking No. 2 in Kiley McDaniel's free agent rankings, and has been the object of serious affection -- perhaps none greater than the Philadelphia Phillies' interest," Passan writes.

The Phillies are reportedly the team showing the most interest in signing Sato this offseason. That's some incredibly exciting news for the Phillies' fan base.

Adding offensive firepower in the form of Sato, the 27-year-old corner infielder and corner outfielder, would make a lot of sense.

If there was one holdup, it would be that Sato is a left-handed hitter, and that the Phillies have not once ever signed a player straight out of Japan to their MLB roster.

But if there was ever a time to break into the Japanese free agent market, it would be now with Sato. He won't hurt them by losing a draft pick if he signs, and he'd instantly provide an offensive upgrade this offense so desperately needs.

Sato wouldn't fix the issues against left-handed pitching, but the Phillies could look to a different free agent or trade option to fill that hole. Besides, maybe Aidan Miller comes up and is an instant star for this team as a righty hitter.

The Phillies need someone like Sato, and this report, noting that they're more interested in him than any team in Major League Baseball, is incredibly exciting.

Dave Dombrowski and the Phillies have a lot of interest in Sato, and now the only question will be: can they meet his asking price, and will Sato choose the Phillies as the first player to sign straight from Japan to the Phillies MLB roster?

articles.title: Mariners reportedly acquire Maikel Garcia from Royals in exchange for 3 pitchers, including Bryce Miller
articles.summary: Maikel Garcia experienced an offensive breakout in 2025.
articles.body:
The Seattle Mariners are looking to add more offense after the team fell short of expectations last season . To address that need, the Mariners reportedly acquired third baseman Maikel Garcia in a trade with the Kansas City Royals, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan.

Seattle is reportedly giving up three pitchers in the deal, including Bryce Miller.

The Mariners are looking to rebound at the plate after the team saw multiple players regress in 2026. Both Cal Raleigh and Josh Naylor experienced significant regression, with Raleigh going from an MVP candidate to one of the worst hitters in the game. In both instances, however, injuries may have played a big role in those struggles. Naylor and Raleigh underwent surgeries this offseason to address various ailments. It didn't help that star outfielder Julio Rodríguez also turned in his worst year at the plate.

Despite those issues, the Mariners' offense still posted a solid 102 wRC+ — an advanced stat that measures a team's total offensive strength — which ranked 10th in the majors. In 2025, the team's offense ranked third in the big leagues with a 113 wRC+. That decline wasn't the only reason the Mariners saw their win total fall from 90 to 76, but it didn't help.

Garcia should help the Mariners regain their 2025 form at the plate, though that's not a guarantee. The 26-year-old experienced a breakout season that year, posting a .286/.351/.449 slash line, with 16 home runs. That was good enough to make him one of the top hitters in the American League.

But multiple injuries sapped Garcia's ability and performance in 2026. He hit just .268/.334/.381 over 82 games. Garcia missed time with a hand issue and various leg injuries throughout the season and never found his groove. His wRC+ fell to 99, marking the third time in four years he's posted a below-average offensive season.

While that's a concern for the Mariners, Garcia should provide value even if his bat doesn't fully recover to his 2025 numbers. Garcia is considered a strong defender, winning a Gold Glove in 2025. He's also capable of swiping bases regularly.

After signing an extension with the Royals last year, Garcia is under contract with the Mariners through at least 2030. The team also has the option to bring back Garcia in 2031 depending on how he performs.

The team also gave up pitcher James McArthur in the deal. He's a 29-year-old righty who hasn't pitched in the majors since 2024.

Garcia's age, performance and contract didn't come cheap. The Mariners had to give up Logan Evans, Jose Ferrer and Miller in the deal.

Over his career, Ferrer has been a solid left-handed reliever. Evans, who missed all of 2026 due to an injury, had an uneven rookie year in 2025, posting a 4.32 ERA over 81 1/3 innings. He struggled to rack up strikeouts in his brief time in the majors.

That makes Miller the crown jewel of the trade for the Royals. The 28-year-old has shown strong skills over his career, though injuries have been an issue. After posting a 2.84 ERA over 180 1/3 innings in 2024, Miller was limited to 90 1/3 innings in 2025 due to elbow issues.

He then injured his oblique in spring training, missing the start of the 2026 MLB regular season. When he returned, Miller looked fantastic over his first 13 starts. During that period, he posted a 2.80 ERA, with 74 strikeouts in 74 innings.

He seemed to lose steam as the year went on, however, posting a 6.45 ERA over his final nine games.

Miller is arbitration-eligible through the 2029 season, so the Royals will have him for multiple years.

The move gives the Royals a possible top-of-the-rotation starter who can carry the load next season until Cole Ragans is ready to return from UCL surgery. Behind those two, the Royals' rotation lacks strikeout upside. The team's rotation combined for a 19.1 strikeout rate last year, which ranked 27th in the majors.

Parting ways with Miller is a risk for the Mariners, but it's also a move the team could afford to make. The Mariners are rife with excellent starting pitchers, to the point where the team often employed a six-man rotation last season to give everyone a chance to start. Trading Miller allows the team to revert back to a five-man rotation, ensuring its best pitchers see the field more often in 2027.

articles.summary: Even though the Texas Rangers are open to exploring Corey Seager trades, his full no-trade clause does complicate the likelihood of a potential move.
articles.body:
Even though the Texas Rangers are open to exploring Corey Seager trades, his full no-trade clause does complicate the likelihood of a potential move.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , Seager is open to a trade only to "a handful of teams" and there is no momentum toward a deal at this point.

The names of those teams were not listed by Passan. Evan Grant of the Dallas Morning News has cited the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox, Atlanta Braves, Philadelphia Phillies as potential fits for Seager.

Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported last week that Rangers officials were going to explore the market for Seager during the general managers' meetings.

The decision to make Seager available comes as the Rangers are projected to have $231 million in payroll obligations for 2027.

Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young told reporters on Nov. 2 the their plan for next season is to keep their payroll "very similar" to the $191.3 million mark from 2026.

In addition to Seager's no-trade rights, the remaining money on his contract also complicates a potential deal. He is owed $193.5 million over the next five years.

Seager hasn't played more than 125 games in a season since his first year with the Rangers in 2022. He's also coming off one of the worst offensive seasons of his career with a .227/.312/.424 slash line.

Next year will be Seager's age-33 season and he has had issues staying on the field throughout his career. The five-time All-Star has played 145 games three times in 12 years.

On a per-game basis, Seager remains incredibly valuable because his defense at shortstop is still very good. He was one of only two players at the position worth at least six defensive runs saved in fewer than 1,000 innings.

Seager could also get some additional credit for being one of the best postseason players of his generation. He owns a .251/.347/.505 slash line and 19 homers in 346 plate appearances in his playoff career, winning World Series MVP in 2020 with the Dodgers and 2023 with the Rangers.

articles.title: Red Sox's Mookie Betts Trade Return Revisited After Connor Wong DFA'd In Wake of Nick Fortes Deal
articles.summary: In the end, the 2020 Mookie Betts trade worked out extremely poorly for the Boston Red Sox. Who could have seen that coming?
articles.body:
In the end, the 2020 Mookie Betts trade worked out extremely poorly for the Boston Red Sox. Who could have seen that coming?

On Wednesday, Boston designated Connor Wong for assignment, the last remaining player on the team's roster from the Betts deal:

In Feb. 2020, the Los Angeles Dodgers acquired Betts and pitcher David Price for outfielder Alex Verdugo, shortstop Jeter Downs—both were considered top-100 prospects at the time—and Wong.

The Dodgers have gone on to win three World Series titles since that trade, with Betts remaining a core member of the roster. The Red Sox have reached the playoffs three times in six years, meanwhile, and haven't won a playoff series since reaching the ALCS in 2021.

Verdugo, 30, spent four seasons (2020-23) with the Red Sox, hitting .281 with 43 homers, 206 RBI, 280 runs and a .761 OPS across 493 games. Calling him a bust would be harsh, though he never lived up to expectations. He then had stints with the New York Yankees (2024) and Atlanta Braves (2025) and signed a minor-league contract with the San Diego Padres ahead of the 2026 season but was ultimately released after requiring season-ending shoulder surgery.

Downs, 28, played all of 14 games for the Red Sox, registering a homer, four RBI and four runs. He hasn't played an MLB game since 2023.

Finally, there's Wong. The 30-year-old stuck around the longest in Boston, appearing in 425 games between the 2021-26 seasons. He ultimately was relegated to backup catcher duties, hitting .243 with 27 homers, 128 RBI, 158 runs and a .676 OPS.

But hey, the Red Sox saved some money! Betts ultimately went on to sign a 12-year, $365 million extension with the Dodgers, well above the $300 million offer Boston reportedly made before trading him to Los Angeles. And those savings only came at the cost of severely straining the organization's relationship with fans by trading an extremely popular superstar for a trio of prospects who never panned out.

articles.title: Sonny Gray Agrees Twins Contract, New MLB Rumors on Free Agency Deal After Red Sox Stint
articles.summary: Veteran starting pitcher Sonny Gray agreed to a two-year, $55 million contract with the Minnesota Twins, according to the New York Post's Jon Heyman.
articles.body:
Veteran starting pitcher Sonny Gray agreed to a two-year, $55 million contract with the Minnesota Twins, according to the New York Post 's Jon Heyman .

Jeff Passan of ESPN reported the second year is a player option. Gray previously played for the Twins from 2022-23.

Gray put together a strong season with the Sox, who acquired him last fall from the St. Louis Cardinals. In 29 starts, he went 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA and 3.47 FIP. He averaged his fewest strikeouts per nine innings (7.9) since 2016 but did a good job of avoiding walks and big contact.

Early into the year, it looked like Gray's time in Boston could be brief.

The Red Sox fired manager Alex Cora and five other staffers in April amid a 10-17 start. Through mid-June, they were 14 games under .500. If the team had been a seller at the trade deadline, Gray was the most likely candidate to go thanks to his age, performance level and contract status.

Instead, the Red Sox caught fire before the All-Star break and continued their hot streak once the season resumed. Once they became a playoff contender, trading Gray was a nonstarter.

As the season progressed, the focus then shifted to his 2027 mutual option.

A $30 million salary is on the higher end for a starter, especially one who will be 37 on Opening Day. Gray, for his part, could prefer to have more long-term financial security, knowing the state of this year's free-agent class.

Tarik Skubal is the crown jewel of the pitching market, but his asking price is going to significantly shrink his candidate pool. Beyond the two-time Cy Young winner, the caliber of available arms falls off quickly.

Freddy Peralta had a terrible start with the New York Mets, and his second half with the Tampa Bay Rays was still a downgrade from his time on the Milwaukee Brewers. Michael King has had two fully healthy seasons as a starter. Then you move into the next tier occupied by Trevor Rogers and Clay Holmes.

Gray had some leverage to command a bigger overall payout than his option, and he'll have the flexibility to test the market again if he puts together another strong season.

articles.title: MLB's Rob Manfred Discusses CBA Talks, 'Can't Imagine' Owners Will Budge on Salary Cap, Floor
articles.summary: MLB commissioner Rob Manfred doesn't believe that team owners are willing to finalize a new collective bargaining agreement that doesn't include a salary cap as well as a salary floor.
articles.body:
MLB commissioner Rob Manfred doesn't believe that team owners are willing to finalize a new collective bargaining agreement that doesn't include a salary cap as well as a salary floor.

"I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred said Wednesday, per Evan Drellich of The Athletic.

On Nov. 3, MLB proposed a collective bargaining agreement containing a salary cap and floor that would be implemented in 2028.

The proposal also included a cap of $258.2 million, while the floor would be set at $180.2 million.

"The projected cap and floor payrolls for 2028 would make 12 clubs increase payroll by $636M to reach the floor, and 8 clubs to decrease payroll $528M to reach the cap," the league said as part of a statement released on Nov. 3. "Overall, this would net a $108M payroll increase. Starting in 2028 would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits."

Both the salary cap and salary floor increased compared to MLB's initial CBA proposal, which contained a $245.3 million cap and a $171.2 million floor beginning in 2027 (h/t MLB.com's Mark Feinsand ).

Players have pushed back against the introduction of a salary cap, with MLB Players Association interim executive director Bruce Meyer weighing in on negotiations on Tuesday.

"At the end of the day, this is going to come down to the bargaining table, and we have been for months, since May, looking for a serious partner in negotiations and the league has insisted since May that they won't negotiate over anything economic outside of our agreement to a salary cap." Meyer said, per Michael Silverman of the Boston Globe . "In that respect, we've wasted months of time when we could have been having a serious negotiation. So I'd say the more the league is focused on things other than bargaining with us in good faith, I would say that's counterproductive."

Manfred isn't willing to reach a compromise that doesn't include a salary cap and floor, though.

"There's plenty of room for compromise, but there's one thing that I will not compromise and that's the issue that we're hearing from the vast majority of our fans: They want a salary cap and floor and on that we will not compromise," Manfred said Wednesday, per Ronald Blum of the Associated Press. "We are not prepared to tell 70 percent of our fans that they're wrong on this issue. Competitive balance is a serious problem, and it needs to be addressed and it's one that we can't avoid just because the negotiation may be difficult."

The current CBA will expire on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET.

If both sides can't reach an agreement before then, it could result in a lockout that threatens the beginning of the 2027 MLB season.

articles.title: Rob Manfred says MLB owners won’t compromise on a salary cap, leaving sport headed to a lockout
articles.summary: Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred said owners will not move off their demand for a salary cap, leaving the sport on track for a lockout starting Dec. 2 that could threaten the 2027 season.
articles.body: Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred said owners will not move off their demand for a salary cap, leaving the sport on track for a lockout starting Dec. 2 that could threaten the 2027 season. “I can’t imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor,” he said Wednesday at a news conference during an owners meeting. Players say they will never accept a cap. The last time management proposed a cap in 1994, it led to a 7 1/2-month strike that caused cancellation of the World Series for the first time in 90 years. “There’s plenty of room for compromise, but there’s one thing that I will not compromise and that’s the issue that we’re hearing from the vast majority of our fans: They want a salary cap and floor and on that we will not compromise,” Manfred said. ”We are not prepared to tell 70% of our fans that they’re wrong on this issue. Competitive balance is a serious problem, and it needs to be addressed and it’s one that we can’t avoid just because the negotiation may be difficult.” Baseball’s five-year collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. EST on Dec. 1. A lockout, which would be the sport’s 10th work stoppage since 1972, would bring to a halt all trades and signings. “A decision on a lockout is one that we’re going to make at the last possible moment,” Manfred said. ”We’re going to devote ourselves to the bargaining process. I’m not that big on Thanksgiving as a holiday. We’ll make ourselves available whenever and wherever to bargain in an effort to make an agreement.” MLB proposed the sport adopt a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028 and a floor of $180.2 million, using luxury tax payrolls with average annual values. A team would be allowed to remain as low as 90% of the floor in 2028, which would be $162.18 million, but would have to spend the entire amount of the floor over a three-year period. Individual contracts also would be capped under the plan, which MLB says includes a 50-50 split of revenue. The union takes issue with management’s definition of revenue and expenses. Players have called the salary cap a “non-starter.” “We made the proposal way back in May. Another word for ‘non-starter’ over months is a refusal to bargain,” Manfred said. “I think it’s time that the MLBPA needs to realize that this proposal is serious. I’m not suggesting they need to accept it whole cloth. I think they need to look at the proposal and try to find some ways to move to the middle as opposed to making no proposal at all.” Players proposed a “competitive integrity tax” that would penalize teams dropping below a payroll floor. They also asked for a rise in the luxury tax threshold and increased salary arbitration rights. “The MLBPA wants more and its proposals undermine, further undermine the competitive quality of our game,” Manfred said. “What has the MLBPA done? They’ve engaged in a lot of rhetoric,” he added. “They’ve characterized our proposals as not real or not serious. They’ve criticized and mischaracterized aspects of the cap and floor system in an effort to promote player opposition. What the MLBPA has not done is made any meaningful effort to move towards us. In fact, they have not made a significant economic proposal since their opening proposal. Indeed, there’s a paucity of responses even on topics that do not directly impact our economics.”

articles.title: With lockout imminent, Rob Manfred 'can't imagine' MLB owners ratifying new CBA without salary cap, floor
articles.summary: The existing collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association is set to expire on Dec. 1.
articles.body:
"I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," MLB commissioner Rob Manfred told reporters at a news conference Wednesday during the league's owners meetings.

While the owners want to introduce a salary cap to a sport that's famously gone without one throughout its decorated history, the players have been staunchly against a cap system for decades.

That dichotomy is at the crux of labor negotiations that appear headed for overtime. The existing CBA will cease at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. If a new deal isn't struck by then, owners are expected to start a lockout. Doing so would put a halt to the MLB offseason and potentially threaten the 2027 campaign as a whole. It would also mark the sport's 10th work stoppage since 1972, according to The Associated Press .

Bruce Meyer, interim executive director of the MLBPA , put out a statement later on Wednesday, responding to Manfred's remarks.

"There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," Meyer said in that statement, via The Athletic's Evan Drellich. "There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries."

"There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," Meyer said in that statement, via The Athletic's Evan Drellich.

"There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries."

Of course, MLB is framing its side of things differently. On Wednesday, when explaining the owners' reluctance to budge on their controversial proposal, Manfred cited the need for competitive balance and fan dissatisfaction, claiming that 70% of fans "want a salary cap and floor."

"And on that, we will not compromise," Manfred said, via SNY .

MLB, as reported by the AP , is pushing for a hard cap of $258.2 million and a floor of $180.2 million for 2028. The proposal reportedly details that teams would be responsible for spending the entire amount of the floor over a three-year span but could use a minimum of 90% of it in 2028.

Under that system, individual contracts would be capped, too.

The last time a cap was proposed, a seven-plus-month strike threw a wrench in the 1994 season. For the first time in 90 years, the World Series was canceled.

"The salary cap and floor are not the real culprit here," Manfred said on Wednesday, according to The Athletic . "The problem the last time, and a big part of the problem now, is that the MLBPA wants more, and its proposals undermine — further undermine — the competitive quality of our game."

Among the players' proposals, per the AP, are the request for a "competitive integrity tax" — which reportedly would punish clubs that dip below a payroll floor — a rise in the luxury tax threshold as well as increased salary arbitration rights.

MLB and the MLBPA have been regularly in talks since May; however, those have been mostly unproductive.

Generally, players are prohibited from reaching the open market for six seasons after their Major League debut. Given that most players reach their physical peak at around 26–27, often, reaching free agency at around 30 means the team that drafted, or signed, and then developed that player already had control of the ascendant stage of their career. articles.title: New Kaima Taira Rumors Update Mets' Pursuit Amid Tarik Skubal Buzz in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The New York Mets are planning to meet virtually with Japanese pitcher Kaima Taira, according to the New York Post's Jon Heyman.
articles.body:
The New York Mets are planning to meet virtually with Japanese pitcher Kaima Taira, according to the New York Post 's Jon Heyman .

The team is casting a wide net in its search for pitching. ESPN's Jeff Passan reported the Mets are viewed as the favorites to land two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. New York is also making a run at Japanese high school prospect Shoki Oda.

In terms of addressing needs, president of baseball operations David Stearns appears to be taking a much narrower focus compared to last offseason. The pitching staff is a clear priority.

Sean Manaea and Kodai Senga both struggled, and the Mets won't want to overtax young arms Nolan McLean and Zac Thornton.

For New York and others, Taira is a particularly attractive target because has been equally effective in NPB as a starter and a reliever.

The right-hander logged 146 innings for the Seibu Lions in 2026, going 12-5 with a 1.36 ERA and posting 141 strikeouts to 45 walks. In 2025, meanwhile, he came out of the bullpen and posted a 1.71 ERA over 52.2 innings.

ESPN's Kiley McDaniel noted Taira doesn't look imposing because of his 5'8" frame but possesses projectable tools:

"From another perspective, Taira has what the sharper pitching organizations seek, with enormous extension, a lower arm slot, short in stature (but with strength), and four-seam ride combining to make a really good fastball shape, which averages 94-97 mph and hits 99-100 mph at times. That's a potentially dominating pitch, as his command is starter quality."

Especially if they sign Skubal, the Mets might value Taira's versatility very highly. He could open the year in the bullpen, where New York definitely requires upgrades, and transition into the rotation as starters inevitably go down.

Come playoff time, Taira could be an even bigger asset.
